label: The Rauch Comparison Theorem
notes: This chapter, printed pages 210 through 241, asks how sectional curvature controls the spreading of geodesics. The engine is the Jacobi field: by comparing its growth against constant-curvature models we read off conjugate points, the exponential map, and metric ball sizes from curvature bounds alone.

label: Jacobi Fields Encode Spreading
notes: A Jacobi field measures the separation between infinitesimally close geodesics emanating from a point. Its norm grows or contracts according to curvature through the Jacobi equation. Comparison theory turns this differential equation into inequalities by bracketing the curvature term between two constants.

label: Constant Curvature Models
notes: On spaces of constant curvature the Jacobi equation decouples into a scalar equation whose solutions are sine, linear, and hyperbolic sine. These three model functions are the yardsticks: every Jacobi field on a variable curvature manifold is compared against one of them according to its curvature bound.

label: The Index Form
notes: The index form is the second variation of energy restricted to vector fields along a geodesic. It is the bilinear quantity that detects conjugate points, and the Rauch theorem is proved entirely by comparing index forms of two manifolds, so we record its definition and sign conventions carefully here.

label: Statement of the Rauch Theorem
notes: The Rauch comparison theorem states that if the sectional curvature of one manifold dominates that of another along corresponding geodesics, then its Jacobi fields are shorter. Greater curvature suppresses spreading; smaller curvature lets geodesics fan out and delays the first conjugate point.

label: The Index Comparison Argument
notes: The proof compares the index forms of the two Jacobi fields after normalizing their initial data. The minimizing property of Jacobi fields among fields with the same boundary values, together with the curvature inequality, forces the ratio of squared norms to be monotone, yielding the comparison.

label: Curvature Bounds the Spread
notes: Picture two geodesic pencils from a point. Under an upper curvature bound the rays separate at least as fast as the lower constant-curvature model; under a lower bound they separate at most as fast. This is the geometric content read straight off the Jacobi field magnitudes.

label: Conjugate Points Comparison
notes: Because curvature controls Jacobi field zeros, an upper curvature bound pushes the first conjugate point no nearer than the model distance, while a lower bound brings it no farther. Smaller curvature therefore postpones conjugate points, a corollary used to bound injectivity and prove manifold theorems.

label: Bounding Jacobi Field Norms
notes: Integrating the monotone ratio yields explicit two-sided bounds: the Jacobi field norm is squeezed between the sine, linear, and hyperbolic-sine model solutions chosen by the curvature bracket. These inequalities are the quantitative heart of every comparison estimate that follows in the chapter.

label: Comparison of Metric Balls
notes: Since the exponential map differential is governed by Jacobi fields, bounding their norms bounds how the exponential map distorts volume. Lower curvature yields larger metric balls and faster volume growth; upper curvature yields smaller balls, giving the Bishop-type volume comparison estimates.

label: Corollaries and Applications
notes: The theorem yields the conjugate point estimates of Bonnet and the spreading bounds used in the sphere theorem and Cartan-Hadamard. We list the principal corollaries: bounds on conjugate distance, on the exponential map being a local diffeomorphism, and on comparison of geodesic triangles.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We recap the chain: curvature bounds enter the Jacobi equation, the index form compares solutions, and the result bounds spreading, conjugate points, and ball sizes. This comparison machinery is the foundation for the global theorems on curvature and topology developed in later chapters.
